Stir in adrak-lehsan paste, all dry spices. Bhuno 3 minutes. Stir in tamatar and cook down 8 minutes.

Cover tightly and cook on medium heat 25-30 minutes until chicken is cooked and very tender.
Stir in hari mirch and garam masala. Increase heat and cook uncovered 5-8 minutes until oil rises to surface — this 'oil on top' is the dhaba signal that the dish is done correctly.

Stir in adrak-lehsan paste, all dry spices. Bhuno 3 minutes. Stir in pureed tamatar.
Stir in bone-in chicken pieces. Bhuno 8-10 minutes on high heat until well-coloured. Season with salt.
Reduce heat. Stir in whisked yogurt gradually. Once incorporated, cook on medium 5 minutes.
Stir in 1/2 cup water. Cover handi tightly — traditional handi cooking is sealed. Cook 25-30 minutes on medium-low until chicken is fully cooked and tender.
Uncover, Stir in slit hari mirch, garam masala, and half the hara dhania. Stir gently. Cook uncovered 5 minutes to desired consistency.

instructions: Get your karahi smoking hot on highest flame. Stir in oil and wait until it's shimmering and almost smoking. Dhabas cook on gas burners the size of your torso — we compensate with patience and maximum heat.
Stir in ginger garlic paste directly to hot oil and Cook aggressively for 2-3 minutes, scraping constantly.

instructions: Warm oil in a large karahi or heavy wok on HIGH flame until shimmering hot. This high heat is the soul of Karachi karahi — don't be shy.

Stir in sliced onions and Cook on high heat until golden brown, about 5-7 minutes, stirring constantly. Stir in ginger garlic paste and Cook for 2 minutes until the raw smell disappears and it turns slightly golden.

Crank heat to high for the last 3-4 minutes to dry out excess moisture. Garnish with ginger juliennes and fresh coriander.

variants.name: Lahori Chicken Karahi

ingredients.text: 0.5 cup Tel or Desi Ghee (Oil or Ghee)
1 tsp Lal Mirch Powder (Red Chilli Powder)

instructions: Put your karahi (wok) or a heavy, deep frying pan on the stove and crank the heat to HIGH. Stir in the tel or ghee (oil or ghee).

Immediately Stir in the roughly chopped lehsan (garlic) and HALF the julienned adrak (ginger) — keep the other half aside for raw garnish later. Stir constantly for 30 seconds. If it's colouring too fast, pull the karahi off the heat briefly.
Stir in all the murgi (chicken) pieces at once. Yes, all of them — the high heat can handle it. Using a large chamcha (ladle) or tongs, stir and turn the pieces constantly for 5 minutes.

Throw in the roughly chopped tamatar (tomatoes), namak (salt), lal mirch powder (red chilli), and dhania powder (ground coriander). Stir everything together well. Keep the heat HIGH — this is not a gentle simmer situation.

Once the tel has clearly separated from the masala, Stir in the slit hari mirch (green chillies) and crushed kali mirch (black pepper). Stir and cook for another 3-4 minutes. The hari mirch will blister slightly and their fresh heat will perfume the dish.
Turn off the heat. Scatter the remaining raw julienned adrak (ginger) over the top — DO NOT stir it in. The adrak sits on top, wilting slightly from the residual heat but staying sharp and pungent.

ingredients.text: 2 tbsp Lal Mirch Paste (Red Chilli Paste)

instructions: FRENCH THE BONE — MAKE THE LOLLIPOP SHAPE: Hold a wingette with the larger bone in your non-dominant hand. Using a small sharp knife, cut around the cartilage at the narrow end of the bone — make a circular cut all the way around.

In a large bowl, Mix the ginger-garlic paste, red chilli paste, soy sauce, chilli vinegar, red chilli powder, salt, and red food colour (diluted in 1 tsp water). Mix well into a thick, even marinade. Stir in the Frenched chicken pieces and coat thoroughly — get the marinade.

In a bowl, mix 4 tablespoons cornflour and 2 tablespoons maida. Stir in the beaten egg. Stir in cold water, a tablespoon at a time, stirring constantly until you reach a thick, coating batter — it should cling to a spoon without dripping off immediately.

Remove the marinated chicken from the fridge. Working one piece at a time, dip the meaty end (not the bone handle) into the batter and coat all around the meat ball. If the batter is too thick and clumping, Stir in another tablespoon of cold water and mix.
In a karahi (wok) or deep pot, heat the frying oil to 170-180°C over medium-high heat. If the oil smokes, it's too hot — remove from heat for 1 minute.

Hold each piece by the exposed bone and lower gently into the oil — never drop pieces in as hot oil will splatter. Cook in batches of 5-6 pieces maximum — do not crowd the karahi. Cook for 8-10 minutes total, turning every 2-3 minutes for even colour.

Remove cooked lollipops with tongs and stand them bone-up in a colander or on a wire rack to drain — standing them upright allows oil to run down and off the meaty end rather than pooling. Arrange standing in a circle on a round plate with the bones.

variants.name: Chicken Malai Tikka
instructions: In a bari pyali (large mixing bowl), Stir in the malai (fresh cream), cream cheese, and dahi (yoghurt). Use a whisk or fork to beat them together until completely smooth — no lumps of cream cheese should remain.

Stir in the flavour builders: adrak-lehsan (ginger-garlic) paste, nimbu (lemon) juice, safed mirch (white pepper), chhoti elaichi (green cardamom) powder, javitri (mace) powder, corn flour, oil, namak (salt), and finely minced hari mirch (green chillies). Whisk everything into a smooth, creamy paste.
Cut your chicken breast into large cubes — about 2 inches each. Not too small, or they'll dry out on the grill.
Stir in the chicken pieces to the marinade. Cover the bowl with cling film and refrigerate for minimum 3 hours — overnight (6-8 hours) is ideal.

When you're ready to cook, take the chicken out of the fridge 20 minutes before grilling — this brings it to room temperature so it cooks evenly. Let excess marinade drip off — too much will cause flare-ups on the grill.

CHARCOAL GRILL METHOD (best results): Light your angeethi (charcoal grill) and let the coals turn ash-white — this means they're at the right temperature: hot but not raging. Cook for 3-4 minutes per side, turning every few minutes. You're looking for gorgeous brown char spots — not blackened.
During the last 3-4 minutes of grilling, baste each piece with melted makkhan (salted butter) using a brush or the back of a chamcha (spoon).

OVEN METHOD (if you don't have a grill): Preheat your oven to 220°C (425°F). Cook for 18-20 minutes, turning once halfway. and then switch to the broil/grill setting and blast the top for 3-4 minutes to get those char spots.

instructions: Prepare the chicken marinade: In a large bowl, Mix 1⁄2 cup thick dahi (yogurt), 2 tbsp Shan Tikka Masala, 1 tbsp adrak lehsan paste, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tsp laal mirch powder, 1⁄2 tsp garam masala, and 1 tsp zeera powder. Whisk until smooth and well-blended. The.

Stir in 600g boneless chicken cubes to the marinade. The yogurt should cling to the chicken — if it looks too runny, Stir in 1 tsp of cornflour (cornstarch) to bind it. Cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, ideally 6–8 hours.

In a blender, Stir in 1 cup packed hara dhania (fresh coriander), 1⁄2 cup packed podina (mint leaves), 3–4 hari mirch (green chillies), 1 tsp whole zeera, 1⁄4 cup dahi, 1 tbsp lemon juice, and 1⁄2 tsp namak. Blend until smooth, scraping down the sides as needed. If.
Put in a bowl of ice water with 1⁄2 tsp salt for 15 minutes. Drain well and pat dry with a clean kitchen towel.

Cook the chicken: Heat 3 tbsp cooking oil in a large tawa or non-stick pan over high heat until it shimmers. Stir in the marinated chicken cubes in a single layer — do not overcrowd. Let them sear undisturbed for 3–4 minutes until deeply charred on the bottom.

Optional but traditional — Stir in charcoal smoke (dhungaar): Once the chicken is cooked, make a small well in the centre of the pan. Cover the entire pan tightly with a lid and let the smoke infuse for 2 minutes.

Cook the parathas: If using frozen lachha parathas, cook them according to package instructions on a preheated tawa over medium heat, using ghee for crisping. If making fresh parathas, roll them out thin, brush with melted ghee, fold into the characteristic lachha (layered) shape, and cook on the.

Assemble the roll: Put a hot paratha on a clean work surface or piece of butter paper. Stir in a generous line of the cooked chicken boti, a handful of soaked sliced pyaz, and a few strips of slit green chilli if desired.

instructions: Blend cashews and almonds with 3-4 tablespoons of water until smooth.
Mix yoghurt, nut paste, grated ginger, minced garlic, and all remaining ingredients.

Remove 45 minutes before cooking.

Cook on medium heat, 12-14 minutes per side for bone-in. Like malai tikka, Afghani tikka should not be cooked on high heat — the nut paste and yoghurt burn easily. Baste with oil or butter every 3-4 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes.

Each side will take approximately 5-7 minutes to cook, depending on the intensity of your broiler.

ingredients.text: 2 tbsp kashmiri mirch (Kashmiri red chilli powder)

instructions: Mix yoghurt, Kashmiri mirch (this is the colour hero), regular chilli, ginger garlic paste, all dry spices, oil, and lemon juice. Mix well — the marinade should be thick, red, and aromatic.
Coat chicken thoroughly, pushing marinade into the cuts. Cover and refrigerate for minimum 4 hours — overnight is the Karachi restaurant standard.
Take chicken out 30 minutes before cooking.
Cook on charcoal grill or under maximum oven broiler. Coal grill: 8-10 minutes per side, turning once. Oven broil: 12-15 minutes per side.
Put lit coal piece in a small foil cup, drizzle few drops of oil to make it smoke, Put cup with chicken, cover tight for 3 minutes. This one step replicates the coal grill flavour at home.
Rest 5 minutes.

variants.name: Lahori Chicken Tikka

ingredients.text: 2 tbsp Adrak Lehsan Paste (Ginger Garlic Paste)
2 tsp Lal Mirch (Kashmiri Red Chilli Powder)

instructions: In a large bartan (bowl), mix the salt, nimbu (lemon) juice, and adrak lehsan paste. Leave for 20 minutes at room temperature.

In the same bartan, Stir in the dahi (yoghurt), tikka masala, Kashmiri red chilli powder, haldi (turmeric), and oil. Mix well into a thick, smooth paste. Coat the chicken pieces thoroughly in this mixture, making sure it gets into all the cuts.
Remove the marinated chicken from the fridge 30 minutes before grilling.
Put chicken pieces on the hot grill, leaving space between each piece — don't crowd. Close any grill lid if you have one. Cook for 8-10 minutes without touching, and then turn with tongs.
Arrange the cooked tikka in a deep metal bowl or pot. Cover immediately with a lid and let the smoke work for 60-90 seconds.

Let the tikka rest for 3-4 minutes before serving — this allows the juices to redistribute through the meat. The tikka should smell smoky and spiced, the surface should have visible char, and the meat should be juicy when you cut into it. Anything less and the grill.

Remove from fridge 45 minutes before cooking. Pat off any excess marinade from the surface — too thick a layer can prevent proper charring.

variants.name: Pakistani Chowmein (Desi Chinese Hakka Noodles)

ingredients.text: 300 g Hakka Noodles or Egg Noodles

instructions: Bring a large pot of water to a full rolling boil. Cook the noodles for 1 minute LESS than the package instructions say. Drain immediately and run cold water over them to stop cooking.
Mix the sauces together in a small bowl: dark soy, oyster sauce, chilli garlic sauce, white vinegar.
Warm 1.5 tbsp oil in your largest wok or frying pan on MAXIMUM heat. Let the oil smoke slightly before you Stir in anything. Stir in the sliced chicken strips and spread them out in one layer.

Stir in the remaining 1.5 tbsp oil to the same hot wok. Stir in the ginger-garlic paste and green chillies immediately. Stir-Cook for 30-40 seconds, keeping them moving, until the paste turns from pale yellow to golden and smells nutty and fragrant rather than raw.

Throw in the carrot first (it takes longest to cook), stir-Cook for 60 seconds. Stir in the cabbage and capsicum, toss everything on maximum heat for another 90 seconds. You are looking for some charred edges on the cabbage, which means your heat is high enough.
Stir in the cooked, cooled noodles to the wok. Immediately pour the sauce mixture over the top. Cook on high heat, tossing continuously, for 2 full minutes.
Return the cooked chicken to the wok, toss for a final 30 seconds just to heat it through and integrate. Transfer to a large plate or bowl immediately.

instructions: Bring a generous amount of water to boil and Stir in a few fat pinches of salt. Season the chicken pieces well with salt, pepper, and a tiny pinch of cayenne (red chilli powder).

Stir in the cheese, tossing the pasta frequently as you Stir in it. It should melt into the pasta fairly quickly, Stir in a splash of pasta water and additional cream to loosen the sauce if needed. Cook on medium heat stirring frequently until the sauce is a consistency you like. If it thickens too much and then Stir in more pasta.

In a small stockpot or large heavy saucepan over medium heat, Stir in the oil. Stir in the onion, stirring occasionally until it begins to turn golden, 6 to 8 minutes.

instructions: Warm oil in a heavy bottomed pot. Stir in the cumin seeds and whole black pepper.
When the cumin seeds start to sizzle and then Stir in the onions. Cook on medium heat stirring occasionally until the onions are mostly a rich brown.

Stir in the garlic paste, saute for a minute and then Stir in the red chili powder, turmeric, coriander powder and salt. If at any time during the process the spices or onions start to burn Stir in a splash of hot water.

Cook stirring frequently for about a minute and then Stir in the chicken pieces, stirring them at regular intervals until the look cooked/white from all sides. Pour 1.5-2 cups of hot water into the pot, bring to a boil and and then simmer covered for 30 minutes.

Increase the heat and dry up the masala, as you do so the onions will break down and form a beautiful cohesive paste. Once the masalas become a paste and the oil rises to the top (bhunn) and then Stir in hot water as per your preference along with the green chilies and bring the mixture to a boil.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: Turn the heat to medium and Put a heavy-bottomed pan, (I use a 6 qt stockpot) on the stove. Stir in oil and allow pan to heat up for 2 minutes.
Stir in onions and saute till they start to turn golden. At this point, Stir in the fresh garlic and ginger and continue to sauté.

This will take a total of 15 minutes. Stir in tomatoes, salt, chili pepper and turmeric and turn the heat to medium or medium-high, start to "Cook" (bhuno) this mixture. Be careful, the tomato sauce may splatter, in that case, turn the heat down. It will take approximately 15-20 minutes.

Let the mixture cool a bit and transfer the chunky ingredients with a slotted spoon, to a blender. Blitz it all to a smooth paste, Stir in some water to the blender if Aim for to get all the sauce off the walls of the blender.
Transfer mixture back to the pan. Stir in chicken pieces and 1/2 cup of water and turn the heat to medium-high.

"Cook" (bhuno) the chicken till you start to see the oil separating from the sauce. This will take approximately 15-20 minutes and rigorous stirring. Stir in the remainder of the water- 1 1/2 cups and cardamom pods, turn the heat to low, cover with a lid and let it simmer for 20 minutes.
Serve with a garnish of fresh chopped coriander/cilantro, (both leaves and sweet stems), kachumbar and chapati or Basmati rice.

instructions: Measure 1 cup of urad dal into a bowl and rinse it with cold water 3–4 times, swirling it with your fingers until the water runs mostly clear. Cover with plenty of cold water (at least 3 cups — the dal will expand) and leave it to soak.
Drain the soaked dal completely — shake off as much water as you can. Transfer to a blender or a mixer-grinder (mixie). Stir in the ginger piece, green chilli (if using), and 1 tsp salt.

Pour enough oil into a karahi (wok) or deep pateela (saucepan) to give you at least 3 inches of depth — you need the baray to float and Cook without touching the bottom. Heat the oil over medium-high heat. If it burns instantly, reduce the heat slightly.

Using a wet tablespoon or wet fingers (keep a small bowl of water nearby to dip your hand or spoon between each one), drop rounded spoonfuls of batter gently into the hot oil. Cook for 4–5 minutes, turning them with a slotted spoon so they colour evenly. They.
Fill a large bowl with warm (not hot, not cold) water and Stir in 1/2 tsp salt to it. Leave them to soak for 20–30 minutes.

After soaking, take each bara one at a time and gently squeeze it between your palms — gently, like you're squeezing a sponge, not wringing out a towel. Put the squeezed baray in a single layer on your serving platter or in individual serving bowls.
In a bowl, whisk the 2 cups of cold dahi with 1 tbsp sugar and 1/2 tsp salt until it is completely smooth, creamy, and pourable like a thick sauce.
Pour the cold whisked yoghurt generously over the baray — Aim for them completely covered.

The assembled platter will look like a beautiful festival of colour — pale white yoghurt, dark brown imli chutney, bright green hari chutney, and orange-red chilli powder scattered over fluffy white baray.

variants.name: Lahori Dahi Bhalla
instructions: Rinse the dhuli urad dal and moong dal together under cold water until the water runs clear — this removes excess starch. Put in a bartan (bowl), cover with cold water by at least 5cm, and soak for minimum 4 hours, ideally overnight in the fridge.

Drain the soaked dal. Transfer to a blender with the adrak (ginger), hari mirch (green chillies), namak (salt), and just 2-3 tablespoons of paani (water). Blend on high until completely smooth — no grainy texture at all.
Transfer the batter to a large bartan (bowl). beat it vigorously with a chamcha (ladle) or electric hand mixer for 3-4 minutes.
Warm tel (oil) in a karahi (wok) or deep degh (pot) on medium heat — test with a tiny drop of batter: it should rise to the surface within 2-3 seconds. Cook 4-5 at a time.

This is the most important step for Lahori Dahi Bhalla and the one most people skip. As soon as the bhalle come out of the oil, transfer them immediately to a large bartan of warm (not hot) paani (water) with a pinch of namak. Submerge completely and leave.

While the bhalle soak, whisk the dahi (yoghurt) until completely smooth. Stir in half a teaspoon of zeera powder, a pinch of namak, and optionally a teaspoon of chini (sugar) if Aim for the dahi slightly sweet in the Lahori style. Whisk again.
Pour the cold whisked dahi over them generously — enough to half-submerge each bhalla.
Stir in the remaining roasted zeera powder (cumin). Scatter a pinch of lal mirch (red chilli powder) for heat and colour. Stir in a handful of torn hara dhaniya (fresh coriander) leaves.

variants.name: Balochi Dampukht

ingredients.text: 100 grams charbi (sheep or goat tail fat)

instructions: In a heavy-bottomed degh (pot) or large karahi (wok), heat 4 tbsp ghee or oil over medium heat. Stir in 2 of the sliced onions. Cook, stirring every minute, for 15-18 minutes until they are deep golden brown — the colour of dark honey — and some edges.

In a large bartan (bowl), Mix the mutton pieces with full-fat yoghurt, ginger matchsticks, whole garlic cloves, all the whole spices (cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, cumin seeds, bay leaves), half the fried barista pyaz, and salt. Mix thoroughly so every piece of mutton is coated in the yoghurt.
Into the same degh that still has the ghee in it, scatter the third onion (raw, thinly sliced) in an even layer at the bottom.
Mix 2 cups of atta (whole wheat flour) with enough water to make a firm, non-sticky dough — about half a cup of water. Roll it into a long rope, about the thickness of your thumb.

THE FIRST PHASE — HIGH HEAT: Put the sealed degh on your stove over medium-high heat for the first 10 minutes. begin to hear a faint sizzling sound from inside the pot — this tells you the liquid has begun to boil and steam is building up inside.
THE LONG SLOW COOK — DO NOT OPEN: Cook on the lowest possible heat for 2 to 2.5 hours without opening the pot.
After 2-2.5 hours, turn off the heat. Let the pot rest for 10 minutes — this allows the steam pressure to reduce before you open it. The colour will be a warm, pale golden-brown.
No garnish is strictly necessary, but a scattering of fresh green coriander (dhania) and a few thin slices of raw onion alongside adds brightness.

variants.name: Balochi Dampukht Chicken

instructions: Stir in sliced onions and sauté for 3-4 minutes until just beginning to soften. Don't brown — Aim for them to steam, not Cook.
Layer chicken pieces over the onions. Stir in tomato halves, salt, black peppercorns, garlic, ginger, and bay leaves.
Cover tightly with the lid.
Put over lowest heat for 90 minutes. The chicken will cook in its own steam plus the moisture from onions and tomatoes.
At 90 minutes, break the seal. If not quite done, reseal and cook 15-20 minutes more.

variants.name: Balochi Dampukht Mutton

instructions: Rub mutton pieces generously with salt and black pepper. Let rest for 30 minutes minimum — 2 hours in the fridge if time allows.
In a heavy, thick-walled pot (clay is traditional, Dutch oven is excellent), layer: first the ghee, and then sliced onion, ginger, garlic, bay leaves, and black cardamom.
Roll into a rope and press firmly around the entire rim of the pot to create an airtight seal with the lid.

VERY LOW HEAT — HOURS OF PATIENCE: Put sealed pot on the absolute lowest heat possible. Optionally, Put a tawa (flat griddle) between the flame and the pot for even more gentle heat. Cook for 4-6 hours.
After 4 hours, carefully crack the seal slightly and insert a knife through to feel the meat. If there's any firmness, re-seal with fresh dough and cook another 60-90 minutes.
Garnish with hara dhania and serve with lemon wedges.

variants.name: KP Dampukht Beef

In a heavy Dutch oven or clay pot, Stir in ghee. Layer onion, ginger, garlic, black cardamom (crushed), cinnamon, bay leaves.
Put over lowest heat possible, or in 150°C oven. Beef needs longer than mutton — 5 hours minimum, 6 hours for perfect tenderness.
Carefully crack seal and test beef with a knife — must meet zero resistance. Re-seal and cook if needed.
Garnish with hara dhania.

variants.name: KP Dampukht Lamb — Dum-Sealed Pot
instructions: Layer the sliced onions across the bottom.
Put the mutton pieces on top of the onions. Stir in salt, black peppercorns, black cardamom, cinnamon, whole garlic head, and ginger. Do NOT Stir in any water or oil.

Roll out the dough into a long snake and press it firmly around the join between pot and lid, sealing it completely. Alternatively, cover the pot tightly with two layers of aluminum foil, and then Put the lid on top and seal the foil around it.
Put the sealed pot over the lowest possible heat.
Do not open the pot — every time you open it, you lose the accumulated steam and pressure that is doing the cooking.
Once cooked, turn off heat and let rest, still sealed, for 15 minutes.

ingredients.text: 3 tbsp Tuvar Dal (Pigeon Pea / Arhar Dal)

instructions: Soak them together in cold water for 30 minutes while you prep everything else.

In a small, dry tawa (griddle) or frying pan over low heat, dry-roast 2 tsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp cumin seeds, 1 cinnamon stick, 3 cardamom pods, 4 cloves, and 1 star anise. Stir constantly with a chamcha (spoon) for 2-3 minutes until you smell a warm, toasty.

In a large pateela (deep pot) or degh (heavy-bottomed pot), Stir in the drained soaked lentils, kaddu (pumpkin) chunks, chopped methi leaves, chopped tomatoes, and 1 roughly chopped onion. Stir in the mutton pieces on top. Pour in 1.5 litres of water.

Remove the mutton pieces carefully with tongs and set aside in a bartan (bowl). use a hand blender directly in the pateela to blend the dal and vegetable mixture until smooth, OR transfer in batches to a regular blender.

Into your blended dal-and-meat pot, stir in: 2 tbsp tamarind paste, 2 tbsp grated jaggery (gur), and your entire freshly ground Dhansak masala. Stir everything in thoroughly. Bring to a gentle simmer on medium heat.

In a separate small karahi (wok) or frying pan, heat 3 tbsp oil or ghee over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 finely sliced onion. Cook, stirring frequently, for 12-15 minutes until deep golden brown and crispy — what's called barista pyaz.

In a separate pateela, wash 2 cups of basmati rice and soak for 20 minutes. In a small pan, heat 2 tbsp sugar over medium heat without stirring until it melts and turns a deep amber caramel colour — 3-4 minutes. Stir in 2 cups of water carefully.

Give the Dhansak a final stir and taste for salt. The gravy should be thick — thicker than regular dal, almost like a loose stew — and should coat the back of a chamcha (spoon). If it's too thick, Stir in a splash of hot water and stir.

ingredients.preparation: plus additional to adjust seasoning to taste

instructions: Mix all the ingredients except the Hara Masala ones in the Instant Pot along with half a cup water and give it a mix. Close the lid, set to seal and set to pressure for 25 Minutes and then natural release (that means turn the machine off and walk away till the pressure releases, and then open the valve.).

Put the Instant pot on saute mode and saute until the excess moisture dries out and the meat mix begins to stick to the bottom. Mix all the ingredients EXCEPT the green masala ones in a pot with 2 cups of water, bring to a boil and simmer on low for 45 minutes or until the daal is completely tender.

Crank up the heat, dry up excess water, your meat mixture should start to stick. Decision time: for a smooth kabab run the entire meat mix through a food processor (in batches or one go) OR run half of it through a food processor and mix it into the original kabab mix.
Stir in ALL the hara masala, feel free to sneak a taste! Wet your palms and shape the kababs to your preferred size.

Cook A TEST KABAB! Line a tray with parchment paper/plastic wrap and Put your kababs on it as you shape them. Put the tray in the freezer and once the kababs are frozen and then you can transfer them to a freezer safe container or bag.
To Cook: defrost on the counter or in the fridge or microwave and and then shallow Cook on medium high heat for about 1.5 minute per side.

instructions: Put the tukmaria (basil seeds) in a bartan (bowl) with 1 cup cold water. Stir once and leave for 20-30 minutes.
Bring a pateela (saucepan) of water to a boil. Stir in the falooda seviyan and cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they are soft but still have a slight chew.
If using instant mix or bought rabri, prepare as instructed and chill thoroughly. The rabri should be thick enough to pour slowly — not solid, not liquid.

BUILD THE GLASS — LAYER 1 (BOTTOM): Use a tall, wide glass — a milkshake glass or any 400-500ml glass. Start with gulkand (rose petal jam) if using: Stir in 1 teaspoon to the very bottom. and then Stir in the soaked tukmaria (basil seeds) — 2 tablespoons.

BUILD THE GLASS — LAYER 2 (NOODLES AND ROSE SYRUP): Stir in a generous pile of the cooled falooda seviyan (vermicelli) — about 3-4 tablespoons. and then pour 4 tablespoons of Rooh Afza rose syrup over the noodles. Stir in the crushed baraf (ice) — pack it in.

BUILD THE GLASS — LAYER 3 (MILK AND RABRI): Pour the cold doodh (milk) gently over the ice — about 3-4 tablespoons. and then spoon the rabri over in a thick layer — 3-4 tablespoons. Pour it slowly so it sits on top of the milk rather than.
Put one scoop of kulfi or vanilla ice cream on the very top of the glass — this is the crown. Stir in a pinch of dried rose petals if you have them.

The etiquette is to eat the ice cream first with the spoon, and then stir the whole glass gently (just enough to mix, not to fully homogenise) and drink through the straw. Do not let a falooda sit for more than 10 minutes before drinking — the ice.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: Stir in basil seeds to 1 cup cold water. Stir and leave for 30 minutes — they expand dramatically into jelly-like pearls. Drain and refrigerate.

Boil water in a small saucepan. Stir in falooda sev and cook for 2-3 minutes until softened but still slightly firm (al dente — it will soften further in the milk). Drain, rinse under cold water immediately, and refrigerate in a small amount of cold water.
Every element must be cold before assembling. Make sure your glasses are chilled too — put them in the freezer for 10 minutes.
In a tall glass, Stir in 1 tbsp rose syrup. Stir in 2 tbsp soaked tukmaria seeds. Stir in 2-3 tbsp falooda sev.
Put a generous scoop of vanilla ice cream on top of the milk.
Stir lightly as you go to mix the layers — that first spoonful of everything together is peak Karachi.

instructions: In a bhari degh (heavy-bottomed pot) or large pateela (saucepan), Stir in the grated gajar and pour in 1 litre of full-fat doodh (milk). Bring to a boil on high heat, stirring frequently with a chamcha (ladle) so the milk doesn't scorch on the bottom. Once boiling, reduce.
Begins the meditation. Cook the carrot-milk mixture on medium-low heat, stirring every 5-7 minutes, for 45-60 minutes.

Once the milk has fully evaporated and the mixture looks thick and jammy with no visible liquid, Stir in 2 tbsp of ghee (clarified butter) and stir it through. Stir in the cheeni (sugar) and the freshly ground elaichi (cardamom) powder. Stir well.

Once the sugar liquid has dried up and the halwa looks shiny and cohesive, crumble in the khoya (dried milk solids). Stir vigorously — the khoya will melt in and make the halwa incredibly rich and fudgy. Cook for another 5 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Stir in the remaining 2 tbsp ghee — this last addition gives the halwa a beautiful gloss and keeps it from drying out as it cools. you can Stir in more cheeni if needed.

instructions: Peel and finely grate carrots using a box grater or food processor. Heat 2 tbsp ghee in a wide, heavy-bottomed karahi over high heat. Pour the milk over the dried carrots and stir well. Cook on medium-high heat, stirring every 3-4 minutes, until all the milk is absorbed — about 20-25 minutes.
Stir in sugar and stir through. The sugar will initially release more moisture — keep stirring on medium heat for another 8-10 minutes until the liquid is reabsorbed and the halwa looks fudgy again.
Crumble in the khoya and Stir in the remaining 2 tbsp ghee. Stir vigorously for 3-4 minutes.
Stir in cardamom powder and fold in the fried raisins and half the almonds. The halwa is done when it holds its shape on a spoon and ghee starts to separate slightly at the edges.

instructions: START WITH THE PANI (make this first so it has time to chill). In a blender, Mix the podina (mint) leaves, hara dhaniya (coriander — stems and all), hari mirch (green chillies), and 1 cup of water. Blend on high until completely smooth — about 30-45 seconds.
Pour the green mixture through a chalni (fine sieve or muslin cloth) into a bari jug (large jug or pitcher).

To the strained green liquid, Stir in the remaining 3 cups of thanda pani (cold water), imli (tamarind) paste, chaat masala, bhuna zeera (roasted cumin powder), kala namak (black salt), regular namak (salt) to taste, and gur (jaggery). Stir well until the gur dissolves completely. Stir in more.

Knead the dough for a full 10 minutes. Yes, 10 minutes. This kneading develops the gluten that gives the puris structure to hold their hollow shape when fried.

Take one portion and roll it out on a lightly floured surface — VERY thin, about 1-2mm. Use a bottle cap or small round cookie cutter (about 4cm diameter) to cut out circles. Gather the scraps, re-knead briefly, and roll again.
Warm the tel (oil) in a karahi (wok) or deep pot to 180 degrees C (350 degrees F).
Cook the purian in small batches (4-5 at a time — do not crowd the karahi). Drain on paper towels or a wire rack.

In a pyali (bowl), Mix the ublay chanay (boiled chickpeas), diced ublay aloo (boiled potatoes), chaat masala, lal mirch (red chilli powder), a pinch of bhuna zeera (roasted cumin powder), and namak (salt) to taste.

instructions: HAND-POUND THE MUTTON — THIS IS THE ENTIRE TECHNIQUE: Cut the mutton (with its fat) into rough chunks. Continue for 15-20 minutes, working in batches.

To the pounded mutton paste, Stir in half a teaspoon of salt, a pinch of ground cardamom, and a pinch of sonth (dry ginger powder). Mix by folding and pressing — not stirring — to incorporate the spices evenly.

In a wide, deep pateela (pot) or degh, bring 2 cups of water to a gentle boil. Stir in the black cardamom pods, cinnamon stick, cloves, and half a teaspoon of salt to the water. Reduce heat to medium-low and poach (not boil) the meatballs for 20 minutes.

In a separate heavy-bottomed karahi or the same pateela (remove the whole spices with a slotted spoon first), heat 3 tbsp ghee over medium heat. Stir in the fennel powder (saunf) and stir for 30 seconds — smell an immediate, beautiful aniseed fragrance rise from the pan. Stir.
Stir in THE YOGHURT — THE MOST CRITICAL STEP: The yoghurt must be at room temperature. Take it out of the fridge 30 minutes before this step. Whisk it smooth in a bartan before adding.

Once all the yoghurt is incorporated and the gravy is smooth and pale, pour in the reserved poaching liquid (the meatball cooking water with the whole spice flavour). Stir to Mix. Bring to a very gentle simmer — tiny bubbles at the edges only, not a full boil.
If it's too thick, Stir in a splash of hot water and stir gently.
Pour the gravy generously over the rice.

Once simmering, cook the yogurt gravy on medium-low heat for 10 minutes, stirring frequently.

The chamcha pounding method is traditional and therapeutic: press, stir, press, stir, for about 10 minutes.

Cook the pounded haleem on the lowest possible flame for another 30 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes to prevent sticking. The haleem should thicken to the point where it coats the back of a chamcha and holds its shape briefly when you push it aside.

Warm 3 tbsp desi ghee in a tiny pan until smoking. Stir in a pinch of lal mirch powder (red chilli) — it will sizzle and turn the ghee a gorgeous red-orange. It adds richness, colour, and a final hit of heat.
Ladle haleem into deep bowls.

ingredients.text: 400 g sabut gehun / gehun ki giriyaan (whole wheat berries/grains)

3 pods hari elaichi (green cardamom for tarka)

instructions: The night before cooking, Put the whole wheat berries in a large bowl and cover with at least 3x their volume of cold water. Leave to soak for 8-12 hours or overnight.

In a large, heavy degh (heavy-bottomed pot), Mix the mutton pieces, chopped onion, ginger-garlic paste, black cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, black peppercorns, turmeric, and salt. Pour in 1.5 litres of cold water. Bring to a boil over high heat, skimming off any grey foam that rises to the surface.

Stir in the soaked and drained wheat grains directly to the pot with the mutton and broth. Stir everything together. If needed, Stir in more water to keep everything submerged — Aim for the level about 2 inches above the wheat and meat mixture.
After 3-4 hours, you'll notice the mixture becoming much thicker. use a heavy wooden spoon or a mathani (wooden masher) to vigorously stir and mash the mixture.

Continue cooking and stirring for another 30-60 minutes after the mashing stage. It should hold its shape for a second when you drop a spoonful onto the surface, and then slowly melt back in. If it's too thick, Stir in a splash of hot water.

Just before serving, heat Raha ghee in a small karahi (wok) or tarka pan over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Stir in the thinly sliced onions and Cook until they are deep golden brown, about 12-15 minutes. Stir in the green cardamom pods in the last minute of.
Immediately pour the hot tarka (ghee, fried onions, and cardamom) over the top — it will sizzle and bubble dramatically. Garnish with julienned fresh ginger and fresh coriander.

instructions: Heat the oven to 180°C and line two trays with baking paper.
Whisk flour, baking soda and salt together.
Beat butter and both sugars for 2–3 minutes until creamy. Beat in the eggs one at a time, followed by vanilla.
Fold in the dry ingredients only until no flour streaks remain, then fold in the chocolate chips.

variants.name: Kaak

ingredients.text: 2 cups atta ya maida (whole wheat or plain flour)

instructions: In a large paraat (wide shallow kneading bowl) or any large bowl, Mix the atta (whole wheat flour) and namak (salt). Mix them together with your hand first, so the salt is evenly distributed through the flour.
Make a well in the centre of the flour. Do not Stir in all the water at once — you may not need the full cup.

Once the dough comes together, transfer it to your clean work surface (a flat counter or marble slab). Knead with the heel of your hand — push the dough away from you, fold it back, rotate, and repeat. Knead for 8-10 minutes.
Shape the dough into a ball, cover it with a damp cloth or invert a bowl over it, and let it rest for 20 minutes at room temperature.
Turn your oven on to 200°C (390°F).

Divide the rested dough into 4 equal portions. Roll each portion into a ball. On a lightly floured surface, use a rolling pin (belan) to roll each ball into a disc approximately 1cm thick and 15-18cm wide.

Carefully Put the discs on your preheated baking stone, cast-iron pan, or a regular baking tray lined with baking paper. Bake for 25-30 minutes. The Kaak is done when it looks pale golden-brown, feels completely dry and hard when you tap it, and sounds hollow when knocked.
Let them cool completely — at least 30 minutes.

instructions: Warm your pot and then Stir in the besan to it and dry roast on medium heat until it smells aromatic. If the colour starts to change and then pull it off the heat immediately. I use an immersion blender because and then I can measure the yogurt in, Stir in the besan and blitz.

Stir in a little oil in the same pot and your curry leaves, methi dana (fenugreek seeds), and ajwain (carom) seeds and saute until fragrant. Immediately Stir in your garlic and dry spices, keep a little water handy in case you need to Stir in a splash to prevent the spices from burning.

Stir in your besan and mix well, it will start to clump up, but don't worry and just whisk the water in. Stir in the green chilies and bring it to a boil and then down to a simmer for 45 minutes., stirring intermittently and scraping the bottom.

Mix the pakora ingredients and start drizzling in the 3/4 cup water mixing well. If you Stir in it all at once it's harder to mix. Warm oil for deep frying (you can pan Cook as well, but and then they don't puff up as much).
Cook a test pakora and taste. The pakoras will expand as they Cook but they will also expand when added to the karhi. Cook for 3 minutes on each side or until deeply golden.

When the karhi is ready Stir in your pakoras, bring it to a boil and turn off. They will simmer in the residual heat. Warm your oil in a frying pan and Stir in the baghaar ingredients, when they are sizzly and aromatic and then pour the baghaar over your karhi.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: In a large bowl, Mix 2 cups sour dahi, 4 tablespoons besan, 1 teaspoon haldi, 1 teaspoon lal mirch, and 1 teaspoon namak. Whisk vigorously until completely smooth — no lumps allowed.
Pour the whisked mixture into a large degh (heavy-bottomed pot) or pateela (saucepan) and Put on medium heat. Stir continuously with a chamcha (ladle) as it heats up.

In a bowl, Mix 2 tablespoons besan, 0.5 teaspoon ajwain, a pinch of namak, and enough water (roughly 3-4 tablespoons) to make a thick batter — it should be thicker than pancake batter, more like a stiff paste that coats a spoon heavily. Stir in your sliced piyaz.
Pour enough tel into a separate karahi (wok) or deep pan to reach about 2 inches deep. Heat on medium-high. If it burns immediately, lower the heat.

Once your kadhi has simmered for 25-30 minutes and thickened slightly, gently Stir in the fried pakoras into the pot. Stir very gently — the pakoras are delicate and you don't want to break them apart. Let the kadhi simmer on low heat for another 10 minutes so.

Warm 4 tablespoons of tel in a small tawa (flat griddle pan) or a small pan on HIGH heat until you can see wisps of smoke. Stir in the methi dana first and let them sizzle for just 10-15 seconds — they burn fast and turn bitter if.
Uncover, give a gentle stir to distribute the tarka, and serve immediately over steamed chawal (rice). Garnish with a sprinkle of fresh hara dhania.

instructions: Have a strong wooden spoon or a heat-resistant silicone spatula ready for stirring.

In a large, heavy-bottomed karahi (wok) or a wide, deep pateela (saucepan) — heavy-bottomed is essential to prevent burning — pour 3 cups of cold water. Stir in 1 cup of cornflour to the cold water. Whisk vigorously with a wire whisk or a fork until the cornflour.

Stir in 2 cups of cheeni (sugar) to the karahi with the cornflour mixture and stir to Mix. Put the karahi over medium heat. and then around 5–7 minutes, it will start to thicken noticeably and look like a pale coloured gel.

When the mixture is thick and gel-like (around 8–10 minutes of cooking), begin adding the ghee. Don't Stir in it all at once. Stir in it in 3–4 additions, about 3 tablespoons at a time, stirring vigorously after each addition until each batch of ghee is fully incorporated.
Continue cooking and stirring on medium heat. This is the long part — it will take 20–30 minutes total from when you started. Watch for these stages: Stage 1 — pale, thick gel (10 minutes).

When the halwa is at Stage 3 (shiny, cohesive, pulling away from the sides), Stir in kewra essence or rose water if using, and stir through quickly. Remove from heat. Working quickly, pour and scrape the hot halwa into your pre-greased tray.

Leave the halwa to cool completely at room temperature — do NOT refrigerate it while it's hot or warm. This takes about 1–2 hours. Once completely cooled and set, use a sharp knife to cut it into diamond shapes: make parallel diagonal cuts in one direction, and then.
Arrange pieces in a single layer or separate layers with parchment paper.

instructions: Warm oil in a large, heavy karahi on medium-high. Cook onions for 10-12 minutes until deep golden brown.
Stir in ginger garlic paste and Cook aggressively for 3 minutes until golden. Stir in turmeric and stir for 30 seconds.

ingredients.text: 1.5 tsp Lal Mirch Powder (Red Chilli Powder)
2 tbsp Adrak Julienne (Ginger Strips for Garnish)

instructions: Put your karahi (wok) or a heavy-bottomed frying pan on the highest flame your stove can produce. Stir in the tel (oil) or rendered fat and let it get smoking hot — see a faint haze rising from the surface.
Stir in the bone-in goat pieces in a single layer — do not crowd the pan. Sear on high heat for 3-4 minutes per side without moving the meat.

Push the meat to the sides of the karahi and drop the pounded lehsan (garlic) and julienned adrak (ginger) into the hot oil in the centre. Stir for 60-90 seconds until the raw smell of garlic disappears and it turns light golden — you'll smell the sweetness kick.
Stir in all the chopped tamatar (tomatoes) at once. Stir everything together, Stir in the lal mirch powder, dhania powder, kali mirch, and half the namak. Turn heat to medium-high.
Once the tomato masala has bhunned (caramelised), increase heat to maximum again. Toss the meat continuously in the masala for 5-7 minutes — this is the most important step.

Stir in the slit hari mirch (green chillies) and the ginger paste (the second half of the adrak you reserved). Toss on high heat for 2-3 minutes. The chillies will blister and soften slightly — they should still hold their shape but have a little give when you.
Take the karahi off heat. Cover loosely with a lid or plate and let it rest for 5 minutes — the residual heat will wilt the dhania and meld the flavours without turning everything mushy.

instructions: In a small katori (bowl), Mix the lukewarm water, 1 teaspoon of sugar (taken from the dough's 2 tablespoons), and the instant yeast. Stir once gently and leave it alone for 8–10 minutes.
In a large paraat (wide mixing bowl) or directly on a clean counter, Mix the maida, remaining sugar, and salt. Pour in the activated yeast mixture, dahi, and oil or melted butter.
Turn the dough onto a lightly floured surface and knead it with the heel of your hand — push forward, fold back, turn, repeat. Keep going for a full 8–10 minutes.
Shape the dough into a ball. Cover with a damp muslin (cheesecloth) or plastic wrap. Put in a warm spot — on top of the fridge, or inside an oven with just the light on — for 1 to 1.5 hours.

In a small bowl, Mix the crumbled or grated khoya, desiccated coconut, raisins, chopped almonds, sugar (for the filling), and cardamom powder. Mix well with a fork or your fingers until everything is evenly distributed.
Set your oven to its maximum temperature — ideally 250°C (480°F). Put a heavy baking tray or pizza stone on the top rack and let it heat for at least 20–30 minutes.

Divide it into 6 equal portions and roll each into a smooth ball. On a lightly floured chakla (rolling board), flatten one ball with your palm, and then use your belan (rolling pin) to roll it into a circle roughly 15cm (6 inches) in diameter.

Gently, very gently, use the belan to roll the sealed dough ball back out into an oval shape about 20–22cm long and roughly 1cm thick. Start from the centre and roll outward in one direction, rotate slightly, roll again.
Carefully pull the hot baking tray out of the oven using thick oven gloves. Bake for 4–6 minutes until the top is golden and has visible brown spots and blisters.

ingredients.text: 800 g Mixed Offal OR Boneless Chicken

instructions: PREP THE OFFAL (if using): If using lamb brain (maghaz): remove the outer membrane carefully (it peels off like a thin skin), and then soak in salted cold water for 30 minutes to remove any blood. Soak kidneys in salted water for 20 minutes to reduce their strong.
Put it on the highest heat your stove allows and let it pre-heat for 3-4 minutes until it's smoking hot. Stir in oil.
Stir in whole cumin seeds to the smoking oil — they'll pop and hiss immediately. Stir in the meat in a single layer (or as close as possible in your pan).

While continuously chopping and stirring, Stir in the ingredients one by one directly to the pan: ginger-garlic paste first (it will splutter — stand back), and then the chopped tomatoes, and then the green chillies, and then the coriander powder, red chilli, turmeric, and salt.

Continue the chopping and stirring for 12-15 minutes on high heat. Everything becomes one cohesive mass — see: patches of caramelised brown char on the meat surfaces, the tomato moisture has evaporated, and the oil has separated and is visible as small shiny pools around the edges.

Reduce heat to medium. If it's too dry and sticking, Stir in 2-3 tablespoons of water and continue stirring — the water will immediately evaporate and help release any stuck bits from the pan (those stuck bits are flavour). A pinch more red chilli if Aim for more.
Turn off the heat.

Stir in the minced beef or mutton keema to the pan. Keep breaking and stirring over high heat. Do not reduce heat.
This is the most important step. Continue cooking the keema over high heat, stirring and pressing, for 15-18 minutes total from the moment the meat hit the pan.

Stir in the hari mirch (green chilli), garam masala, remaining namak (salt), and hara dhania (fresh coriander). Stir to Mix. Transfer to a plate and spread out to cool to room temperature — do not stuff hot filling into the dough.

Put the sealed ball seam-side down on a lightly floured surface. Using a belan (rolling pin), VERY gently roll it out to an oval about 20cm long and 10cm wide. Roll slowly, with even pressure — no sudden heavy pressure that would push the filling through the surface.

Preheat your oven to 250°C (480°F) with a cast-iron tawa (flat griddle pan) or heavy baking tray on the top rack for at least 30 minutes. Bake for 5-7 minutes until the surface is golden with dark spots and the naan feels firm when tapped on the base.

COOK THE KEEMA FILLING — DRY IS THE GOAL: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a small karahi (wok) or frying pan over medium-high heat. Stir in zeera (cumin seeds) — they should sizzle immediately. Stir in the finely chopped pyaaz and cook, stirring, for 5–7 minutes until the.
Stir in the adrak lehsun paste to the golden onion and stir for 1 minute — it will smell sharp and wonderful. Stir in dhania powder, lal mirch powder, and salt. Stir for 30 seconds.

Stir in the minced meat to the pan. Stir and break continuously for 2–3 minutes as the meat changes from pink to grey-brown. Keep cooking on medium-high heat, stirring regularly, until ALL the liquid has evaporated and the mixture looks dry and the meat starts to sizzle in.
Roll one ball into a 12 cm circle.

ROLL CAREFULLY — ONE SIDE ONLY: Dust the filled ball lightly in flour. Roll it out to about 18–20 cm, but here is the special technique for keema paratha: apply pressure from only one direction at a time. Roll outward from the centre, turn 90 degrees, roll outward.
COOK ON MEDIUM HEAT (slightly lower than other parathas): Heat the tawa (flat griddle pan) over medium to medium-low heat.
Transfer to a plate.

Preheat your oven to 150°C (300°F) while the pot is on the stove. After the 15-minute stovetop start, carefully transfer the sealed pot to the middle rack of the oven. Cook for 4 hours undisturbed.
After 4 hours, remove the pot from the oven. If it doesn't, re-seal with fresh dough and return to the oven for another 45 minutes.
Do not serve immediately. Let the Khaddi Kabab rest, uncovered, for 10 minutes.

instructions: Mix yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, all spice powders, salt, lemon juice, and mustard oil. Cover and refrigerate 8-12 hours.
Build a massive charcoal fire inside the pit and let it burn for 2 hours until the rocks are red-hot and the charcoal is glowing embers.
Cover the pit with a heavy metal sheet or wooden boards, and then seal completely with sand or soil.
Leave completely undisturbed for 4-5 hours. The sealed environment creates a convection oven effect — steam and heat circulate and cook the meat from all angles simultaneously.
At 4 hours, carefully open a corner of the seal. If not, reseal and cook 30-60 minutes more.
Transfer to a large thal (serving platter).

instructions: Warm a dry pan on medium heat. Stir in the besan (gram flour) and stir constantly for 3-4 minutes until it smells nutty and turns a shade darker. Spread it on a plate to cool for 5 minutes.
Warm oil in a large pateela (deep pot) on medium-high heat. Stir in 2 finely sliced onions. Cook, stirring regularly, for 12-15 minutes until deep golden-brown (barista).
To the remaining fried onions still in the pateela, Stir in ginger-garlic paste. Stir on medium heat for 2 minutes. Stir in turmeric and red chilli powder — they'll bloom immediately in the hot oil.

Open your coconut milk cans. The thick cream that has risen to the top — scoop that out first and Stir in it to the pot. Stir into the chicken for 2 minutes — the coconut cream will start to Cook slightly and smell intensely coconutty.

Stir in the dissolved besan paste to the simmering coconut curry in a slow stream, stirring constantly as you pour. Once all the besan is incorporated, bring to a full simmer on medium heat and cook for 10 minutes, stirring regularly. You'll see the curry visibly thickening —.
Reduce heat to medium-low, cover the pateela, and simmer for 15-20 minutes until the chicken is completely cooked through. Stir every 5 minutes.

Bring a large pot of salted water to a full boil. Cook spaghetti or noodles according to package instructions minus 1 minute (cook slightly less than stated — they'll continue cooking in the hot curry). Drain, drizzle with a teaspoon of oil, and toss to prevent sticking.

variants.name: Badam Kheer (Almond Milk Pudding)
instructions: The night before, soak almonds in enough water to cover. Reserve a handful of peeled almonds for garnish, and then proceed with the rest.
Stir in the peeled almonds to a blender with 1/2 cup of the milk. Blend on high for 2-3 minutes until completely smooth with no graininess.
Pour the remaining milk into a heavy-bottomed degchi (pot) and bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring occasionally. Once boiling, reduce to a simmer.

Pour the almond-milk paste into the simmering milk while stirring constantly to prevent lumps. Stir in the cardamom powder. Continue to cook on medium-low, stirring every few minutes, for 25-30 minutes until the mixture thickens.
Stir in sugar and stir until dissolved. Pour in the saffron milk — watch the beautiful golden swirls appear. Cook for another 5-8 minutes.
Remove from heat. Stir in rose water and kewra essence. Pour into serving bowls.

instructions: Warm milk and half and half in a large heavy-bottomed pot on the stove (not nonstick).
Bring the mixture to a boil, tear the croissants and rusks into pieces and Stir in them in.
Simmer until both breads are soft, about 5-6 minutes.
Pour back in the pot (if using a regular blender). Stir in the cardamom, saffron, sugar and half the nuts.
Simmer on low heat, stirring frequently, the mixture will darken and thicken.
Cook it down by about 40 percent (nearly half) of what it was –this takes about 20-30 minutes depending on the pot you are using.

variants.name: Caramel Kheer
instructions: Soak basmati rice for one hour in cold water, allowing water to come 3-4cm (or 1-1.5in) above the rice (the rice will expand in water, so Aim for some extra water in the bowl to prevent the rice from drying out). After the rice has soaked for one hour, Put a large, heavy-bottomed pot on the stove on medium-high heat. When the.
Discard cold water from the rice and carefully transfer rice to boiling water with a pinch of salt. The rice will gently boil on medium-high heat. Check rice after 6 minutes.

Stir in milk, cream, and cardamom pods to the rice and starchy liquid. Stir and partially cover the pot with the lid (Aim for a little bit of steam to escape as it simmers, otherwise the milk will overflow). Set your timer to 20 minutes. Stir every 4-5 minutes to ensure that the pudding does not catch at the bottom of the.

At the 20-minute mark turn your stove off, remove the pudding from the burner and stir in the condensed milk (I added 200ml, but you may want to Stir in 250ml). Put in the fridge for 4-6 hours minimum, or overnight.

Put a frying pan on medium-high heat. When the pan is hot, Stir in butter and when it starts to sizzle and turn brown, Stir in breadcrumbs and a pinch of salt and gently stir. When the breadcrumbs have absorbed the butter, Stir in chopped walnuts and stir. Remove from heat and set aside while you prepare the caramel swirls.
Evenly sprinkle sugar in a saucepan and Put on medium-high heat. Remove the saucepan from the heat and allow the sugar to cool for five minutes.
Stir in a dusting of buttered breadcrumbs and walnuts and enjoy.

variants.name: Chawal ki Kheer - Pakistani Rice Pudding
instructions: Boil your rice until it is mushy - this is at least 10 minutes of active boiling.
While that happens use a wide bottomed steel pot (NOT NON STICK) to bring your milk to a simmer.
Lightly bruise the cardamom pods and Stir in them to the milk, keep the temperature low,.
Once the rice is mushy, drain most of the water and and then mash it up thoroughly on a plate with a fork.
Stir in to the milk mixture along with the sugar. Mix well.
Cook on low - a gentle simmer for an hour. Stir with a rubber spatula every and and then to check.
The kheer will cook down quite a bit in this time, Stir in 1/4 cup of the cream you are using and taste - Stir in more sugar or cream if desired.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: Stir in milk and rice to a large pot. Bring to boil, about 3 minutes, and let it simmer on low heat for 40 minutes while stirring often.
Stir in sugar and keep stirring, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the remaining ingredients and let it simmer while stirring for another 8 – 10 minutes.
Put in serving bowl and top with slivered almonds for garnish.

source_attributions.recipe_title: Chawal ki Kheer - Pakistani Rice Pudding

variants.name: Chawal Ki Kheer — Sindhi Slow-Cooked Rice Pudding
instructions: Rinse basmati rice under cold water until clear. Soak in fresh water for 30 minutes minimum.
Pour the full-fat milk into a wide, heavy-bottomed degchi (pot). Stir in the bruised cardamom pods. Bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring occasionally.
Drain the soaked rice and Stir in it to the simmering milk. Stir well. Cook on low heat, uncovered, for 60-75 minutes.

After 50 minutes, the milk will have reduced significantly and the rice will be very soft and starting to break down. The kheer should coat the back of a spoon thickly. If it's too thick, Stir in a cup of warm milk and stir through.
Stir in sugar and saffron milk, stirring until fully dissolved. Cook for another 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in rose water and kewra water if using.
Pour into a serving bowl or individual clay pots (matke) for a traditional Sindhi presentation.

source_attributions.recipe_title: Chawal Ki Kheer — Sindhi Slow-Cooked Rice Pudding

variants.name: Doodh Chawal Kheer — Pakistani Rice Pudding
instructions: Rinse 4 tbsp of chawal (rice) in cold water two or three times until the water runs mostly clear. Soak in fresh cold water for 30 minutes.
Pour 1.5 litres of full-fat doodh (milk) into a heavy bhari degh or pateela (saucepan). Heat on medium-high, stirring frequently.
Once the milk is boiling, Stir in the drained soaked rice. Stir well. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook at a steady simmer, stirring gently every 5 minutes.
This typically takes 45-60 minutes.

Stir in cheeni (sugar) and fresh-ground elaichi (cardamom) powder. Cook for another 5-8 minutes, stirring constantly — the sugar makes the milk slightly thinner momentarily. Stir in the saffron-soaked milk and any crumbled khoya (dried milk solids).
Pour kheer into a large serving bartan (bowl) or individual katoris (small bowls). Serve warm immediately, or cool to room temperature and refrigerate for 2-3 hours.

Warm the ghee or milk as appropriate; toast the grain or simmer the dairy gently so it does not catch.
Add the sugar only after the main ingredient is tender, then cook until the mixture reaches the intended thick consistency.
Stir in the cardamom, saffron or floral water, garnish with nuts if used, and serve at the stated temperature.

variants.name: Quick & Extra-Creamy Instant Pot Kheer
instructions: Grind the rice before you soak it to a coarse grind. Pour over the water and set aside for 20 minutes (or longer).
Put your Instant Pot on sauté and Stir in in your three milks, cardamom seeds, saffron (if using), sugar and salt.
As soon as your sugar dissolves Stir in in your rice + soaking water, give it a quick mix, making sure nothing is stuck to the bottom.
Put your IP on LOW pressure for 18 minutes.
Natural release for 10-15 minutes (to manage the intense steam release), and and then release the remaining steam by turning the valve.
Whisk through to break any clumps, the kheer will thicken as it cools. Transfer to a bowl and garnish as you please.

variants.name: Sewaiyan Kheer (Vermicelli Pudding) for Eid
instructions: Warm ghee in a heavy-bottomed karahi (wok) or pot over medium heat. Stir in the sewaiyan and stir continuously with a wooden spoon. Roast for 4-5 minutes until they turn a deep golden colour and smell nutty.

Pour the full-fat milk into the karahi carefully — it will sizzle. Stir in the lightly crushed cardamom pods. Stir everything together and bring to a boil over medium-high heat, stirring frequently so the milk doesn't catch on the bottom.
Once boiling, reduce heat to medium-low. Cook uncovered for 20-25 minutes, stirring every 3-4 minutes.
Stir in sugar and stir until fully dissolved. Stir in the saffron milk and raisins if using. Cook for another 5 minutes.
Turn off the heat. Stir in rose water and stir gently. The kheer will thicken more as it cools — if it looks too thick, stir in a splash of warm milk before serving.
Pour into a large serving bowl or individual bowls. Serve warm for a cosy Eid morning, or chill for 2-3 hours for a cold, creamy version.

instructions: In a small saucepan, heat 11⁄2 cups of the milk over medium-low heat; do not bring to a boil, but keep warm while you prepare the kheer. In a large heavy-bottomed pan, Stir in the remaining 3 cups of milk, the rice, crushed cardamom seeds, sugar and slivered.

Every 7 to 10 minutes, remove the lid and stir gently, from the bottom up, to ensure that the rice is not sticking to the base of the pan. After about 40 minutes, the milk should be thickened but not entirely absorbed.

If it seems undercooked, Stir in some of the reserved warm milk, replace the lid and continue to cook for 7 to 10 minutes. Transfer the kheer to a container and allow it to come to room temperature before covering and refrigerating at least 5 hours, but preferably.
In a medium saucepan over medium heat, Stir in the rhubarb, cinnamon stick, water and sugar. Stir well.
Allow the mixture to bubble away until the rhubarb looks soft and has melted down into a sauce, about 20 minutes. Stir in the strawberries.
Continue to cook until the strawberries have softened and melted into the sauce, about 10 to 15 minutes.
Turn off the heat, discard the cinnamon stick, and allow the coulis to come to room temperature.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: In a large kunda (mixing bowl) or any wide bartan (vessel), Mix the atta, finely chopped pyaz, hari mirch, hara dhaniya, ajwain, salt, lal mirch, and 1 tbsp of ghee. Mix by hand to mix everything together, working the ghee into the flour — you're looking for a.
Knead the dough on a clean surface for 3-4 minutes until it is firm but not stiff.

Divide the dough into 3-4 equal balls — each about the size of a large lemon. Using a rolling pin, roll it into a circle about 6-7 inches in diameter and about 5-6mm thick (roughly 1⁄4 inch). This is significantly thicker than a roti or paratha — resist.
Warm a tawa (flat cast-iron or heavy pan) over medium-high heat until very hot. Stir in 1 tbsp of ghee and let it heat. Cook for 2-3 minutes.
Stir in another 1⁄2 tbsp of ghee, and then flip the koki.

variants.name: Beef Korma Dawat
instructions: Warm ghee in a large, wide deg. Cook all sliced pyaaz on medium-high for 20-25 minutes, stirring constantly, until very deeply golden-brown. Do not drain — use the same ghee for everything.
Put half the fried onions into a blender with a splash of water and blend to a smooth paste. The other half is reserved for garnish.
In the same ghee, Stir in sabut garam masala, sizzle 1 minute. Stir in onion paste and Cook 5 minutes. Stir in adrak-lehsan paste, dhania powder, lal mirch powder.
Stir in beef pieces, turn heat to high. Bhuno aggressively for 10-12 minutes until well-coloured. Season with salt.
Reduce heat to low. Stir in whisked yogurt 3 tablespoons at a time, stirring constantly between additions. Take your time — 10-12 minutes total to Stir in all the yogurt.
Stir in 1 cup warm water. Cover tightly and cook on medium-low heat for 60-75 minutes until beef is very tender. Check and stir every 20 minutes.
Stir in cashew paste and saffron-milk. Cook uncovered 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until gravy is thick and glossy. Stir in kewra water and gulab jal.

variants.name: Chicken Korma Simplified
instructions: Crush your prefried onions by hand and mix into your yoghurt and set aside.
Warm 1/4 cup oil on medium hight heat and Stir in your dry whole spices - both cardamoms, cloves, black pepper, cinnamon stick, and bay leaf.
Once the spices have perfumed the oil and then Stir in in the ginger and garlic and give it a quick stir.
Stir in in your chicken pieces, turning them periodically until they have all changed colour.
Saute for about a minute and and then Stir in in your yoghurt and onion mix, stirring well to Mix.
Stir in in half a cup of water and bring it to a simmer, cook on low for 25 minutes or until the chicken is cooked through.
Uncover your pan and raise the heat to medium until you see the oil separate from the base for that rich korma taste.
Adjust consistency to your liking and Stir in kewra, garam masala powder, and pepper and adjust seasoning.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: Warm ghee in a wide, heavy pot. Stir in sliced pyaaz and Cook on medium-high heat for 12-14 minutes until golden brown and starting to crisp at the edges. Remove half and set aside for garnish.
Stir in sabut garam masala to the pot with the remaining fried onions. Stir in adrak-lehsan paste and Cook 2 minutes. Stir in dhania powder, zeera powder, and lal mirch.
Stir in chicken pieces and salt. Turn heat to high and bhuno for 7-8 minutes until chicken has changed colour and is well-coated in masala.

Stir in YOGURT — THE CRUCIAL STEP: Reduce heat to medium-low. Stir in yogurt 2 tablespoons at a time, stirring constantly after each addition. Never Stir in cold yogurt straight from the fridge — room temperature is essential.
Once yogurt is incorporated, Stir in 1/2 cup warm water. Cover and cook on low-medium heat for 25-30 minutes until chicken is cooked through and tender. Stir gently every 10 minutes.
If using cashew/almond paste, stir it in along with kesar and crushed green cardamom. Cook uncovered for 8-10 minutes, stirring gently, until gravy is thick and coating the chicken pieces.
Transfer to a serving dish.

variants.name: Safed Korma Mughal

ingredients.text: 1.5 tsp kali mirch (white or black pepper)

instructions: GOLDEN ONIONS — STOP BEFORE BROWN: Heat ghee in a wide, pale-coloured pot (so you can monitor colour accurately). Stir in sliced pyaaz and Cook on medium heat only — no high heat. Cook for 10-12 minutes, stirring constantly, until soft and just turning golden.
Transfer golden onions to a blender. Stir in 2 tablespoons water and blend to a completely smooth, creamy paste.
In the same pot with remaining ghee, Stir in cloves, cinnamon, and crushed green cardamom seeds. Stir in the blended onion paste. Cook gently for 5 minutes.
Stir in chicken pieces and kali mirch. Bhuno gently on medium heat — no high heat that causes browning — for 6-7 minutes.
This is the most delicate moment. Reduce heat to very low. Stir in yogurt 1 tablespoon at a time, stirring smoothly after each addition.
Once yogurt is in, Stir in 1/3 cup water, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 25-30 minutes. The chicken should cook through gently in the creamy yogurt environment.
Stir in cashew paste. Cook uncovered 8 minutes until gravy thickens. Stir in cream, stir gently, cook 3 minutes.

variants.name: Shahi Chicken Korma
instructions: Warm ghee in a deep degh (heavy-bottomed pot) over medium-high heat. Stir in sliced onions and Cook, stirring occasionally, for 20–25 minutes until they turn deep golden-brown — the colour of caramel, not gold.

Return the pot with the reserved ghee to medium heat. Stir in all the kharay masalay (whole spices). Cook for 60 seconds, stirring, until the elaichi (cardamom) puffs slightly and the laung (cloves) begin to uncurl.

Stir in the adrak-lehsan (ginger-garlic) paste to the spiced ghee. Cook for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until the raw smell disappears and it turns light golden. Stir in the chicken pieces and salt.
Stir in this to the chicken along with the ground coriander and cumin. Stir everything together over medium heat for 3–4 minutes until the masala coats the chicken.
Reduce heat to low. Whisk the dahi (yoghurt) until completely smooth — no lumps. Stir in it to the pot one spoonful at a time, stirring continuously.

Stir in the badam (almond) paste — it will immediately thicken the sauce. Stir in 1/2 cup warm water, stir well. Cover the pot and cook on low heat for 20–25 minutes, until the chicken is cooked through and the sauce has deepened to a beautiful golden colour.
Remove from heat. Stir in the gulab jal (rose water) and kewra water. Stir gently.

variants.name: Kulcha
instructions: Mix lukewarm water, sugar, and yeast in a small bowl. Leave 8–10 minutes until frothy.
In a large paraat, Mix flour and salt. Stir in the yeast mixture, dahi, milk, and oil. Mix to form a soft dough — it should be softer and richer-feeling than naan dough.
Oil a bowl, Stir in the dough, cover with a damp cloth, and leave in a warm spot for 1–1.5 hours until doubled.

While the dough rises, Mix the mashed potatoes, chopped onion, fresh coriander, green chillies, carom seeds, salt, and red chilli powder in a bowl. Mix well with your hands until it comes together into a coherent mixture.
Warm for 30 minutes minimum. For a stovetop version, heat a heavy tawa (griddle pan) over high heat until a drop of water dances and evaporates in 2 seconds.

Punch down the dough and divide into 6 balls. On a floured chakla, roll one ball into a 15cm disc. gently roll the stuffed ball out into a thick oval or round about 18–20cm across and about 1–1.5cm thick.

Transfer to the hot baking tray and bake on the top rack for 5–7 minutes until the top is golden and blistered, and the underside is flat and cooked through. For the stovetop method: lay the kulcha on the hot tawa, cover with a lid, cook 3–4 minutes.
Stack them, butter-side up, and cover with a clean cloth to keep warm while you cook the rest.

variants.name: Kulfi Falooda — Classic Street Style
instructions: Pour 1.5 litres of milk into a wide karahi. Bring to a boil, and then reduce to medium heat. Cook, stirring frequently and collecting cream skins to the sides (like rabri-making), for 45-50 minutes until reduced to roughly 600ml.
Remove from heat. Stir in fresh cream, chopped almonds and most of the pistachios. Once cool, refrigerate for 30 minutes until cold.
Pour the cooled kulfi mixture into kulfi molds (conical metal or plastic molds) or into an ice cube tray covered with plastic wrap, or into small steel cups.
Freeze for a minimum of 6-8 hours — overnight is better.
Boil falooda sev for 2-3 minutes, rinse cold and refrigerate. Soak basil seeds in cold water for 30 minutes.

variants.name: Kulfi
instructions: REDUCE THE MILK — THE HEART OF KULFI: Pour all 1.5 litres of full-fat milk into a wide, heavy-bottomed degh (heavy-bottomed pot) or karahi (wok). Bring the milk to a boil on medium-high heat, stirring continuously with a chamcha to prevent it from boiling over.

During the reduction, stir every 4-5 minutes and scrape the malai (cream layer) that forms on the sides and bottom back into the milk. After about 45 minutes, stir more frequently (every 2-3 minutes) as the risk of scorching increases as the liquid reduces.

After 60-75 minutes, check whether the milk has reduced to approximately one-third of its original volume (1.5 litres should become roughly 500ml). Dip a spoon in: the milk should coat the spoon and flow slowly off it rather than running off like water.

Remove from heat briefly. If using cornflour, mix 1 tablespoon cornflour with 2 tablespoons cold milk until smooth, and then stir this into the hot reduced milk. Return to low heat and stir for 2-3 minutes — this helps bind the mixture and reduce ice crystal formation when.
Stir in the coarsely chopped pista and badam. Let the mixture cool completely to room temperature — about 30-45 minutes.

Once completely cooled, pour the kulfi mixture into kulfi moulds (conical metal or plastic kulfi moulds available at any kitchen shop or online). If using cups, cover tightly with plastic wrap, pressing it directly onto the surface of the liquid to prevent ice crystals.
Put the moulds in the freezer and freeze for a minimum of 6 hours. Overnight is ideal — 8 hours gives a firmer, better-set kulfi.
Garnish with sliced pista on top.

ingredients.preparation: whole wheat flour or all-purpose flour
ingredients.text: 2 cups atta ya maida (whole wheat flour or all-purpose flour)
5 tbsp ghee ya makhan (ghee or butter)

instructions: In a large paraat, Mix your flour of choice and salt. Stir in the oil and rub it in with your fingers until the flour looks like wet sand — this is called 'short-shortening' the flour and gives a slightly tender result. Stir in the lukewarm water gradually.
Shape the dough into a ball, cover with a damp cloth or bowl, and rest for 20–30 minutes at room temperature.

On a lightly floured chakla, roll one dough ball into as thin a circle as possible — ideally 2–3mm thick, roughly the size of a medium-large plate (28–30cm). The thinner you roll it, the more layers you will get in your final paratha.
Take the accordion-folded strip and coil it into a tight snail shell shape — starting from one end and winding the strip around itself.

Press the coiled disc flat with your palm — firmly but gently. and then use the belan to roll it out again into a round paratha about 18–20cm across and 5–6mm thick. be able to see the spiral of layers at the edges of the paratha as you.

Warm a tawa (flat griddle pan) or heavy frying pan over medium-high heat until a few drops of water flicked onto it evaporate in under 2 seconds — that is your cue that it is ready. Cook for about 2 minutes on the first side — you will.

After flipping, Stir in about half a teaspoon of ghee to the tawa around the edges of the paratha and let it sizzle underneath. Cook 1–2 more minutes. Flip once more, Stir in another tiny amount of ghee to the other side.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: Mix the atta and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with a dough attachment.
Slowly Stir in in 1 cup of water, letting it mix with the dough before adding more. If the dough seems dry, Stir in the additional 2 tbsp of water.
Continue to knead on medium speed until a smooth, dry, and flexible ball of dough forms.
(It is nice, but not necessary, to let the dough rest for 10-15 minutes to allow the gluten to develop.
Once you are ready to cook the parathas, Put spreadable butter, atta for dusting, and a rolling pin near your workstation.
Meanwhile, heat a tawa, heavy-bottomed (preferably cast iron) or flat griddle over medium heat.
While the tawa is heating, roll the paratha out to 5-6 inches in diameter and spread about 2 teaspoon of butter onto the flattened dough.

Starting from the top, roll down swiss-roll style until a long log is formed. Roll this log, especially from the middle, to make it thinner and as even as possible until it’s about 18 inches long. and then roll tightly into itself from one edge to another.

As the bottom of the paratha begins to cook, Stir in 1-2 tsp of butter to the top. Once the bottom is partly cooked (this will take about 10-15 seconds), use a spatula to flip over and Stir in butter on the other side. Cook on both sides.

variants.name: Lahori Chargha

ingredients.text: 1.5 tsp tatri (citric acid / lemon salt crystals)
1.5 tsp lal mirch powder (red chilli powder)
1 tbsp nimbu ka ras (fresh lemon juice)

instructions: Using a sharp knife, make deep cuts all over the chicken — every 1 inch, cut down to the bone.

In a large bowl, Mix the tatri (citric acid), salt, red chilli powder, coriander powder, cumin powder, turmeric, garam masala, ginger-garlic paste, yoghurt, and lemon juice. Mix everything together into a thick paste.

Rub the marinade all over the chicken — into every cut, under the loosened breast skin, inside the cavity, everywhere. Put the chicken in a large zip-lock bag or cover with cling film and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight (8-12 hours).
Pour 250ml water into the bottom of the steamer. Bring the water to a boil. Cover tightly with a lid, wrapping it in a kitchen towel if needed to trap all the steam.

After 35-40 minutes of steaming, check doneness. If there's any pink, steam for another 10 minutes. Let the steamed chicken rest on a rack for 10-15 minutes and pat the surface as dry as possible with kitchen paper.

Warm 1 litre of oil in a large, deep degh or wok to 180-190°C (355-375°F). Cook for 8-10 minutes, spooning hot oil over the top of the chicken continuously using a large chamcha. The chicken should turn deep mahogany-brown, almost the colour of dark chocolate.

Remove the chargha from the oil using a large slotted spoon or spider strainer and Put it on a wire rack or paper towels to drain for 2-3 minutes. The skin should be deep brown and very, very crispy — it should make a crackling sound when you.

alternate_methods.label: Alternate documented method
instructions: Warm a cup full of water and mix the brown sugar and salt into it. Stir in enough water to cover the turkey. Cover and set aside for 12-24 hours. Take the brined turkey out of the fridge, drain the brine and pat the Turkey dry.
Put the turkey in a dish – you can use the roaster you will roast it in as well. Whisk the marinade ingredients except the butter in a bowl.
Stir in your softened butter. Shmear the rest over the back, legs, and wings of the turkey.

The day you are going to roast the turkey pull it out of the fridge a few hours before roasting to bring it to room temperature. Roast the Turkey till the top is a gorgeous brown colour, some of the masala will look charred and that is delicious. This will take about 30 minutes.

Drop the temperature to 350 F, tent the turkey with foil and roast until a meat thermometer inserted in the thigh reads 170 degrees F, this took me another 1 hour and 50 minutes over and above the initial bake time. Let the turkey meat rest for at least 20 minutes before carving.

instructions: Score the mutton pieces deeply with a sharp knife — cuts about 2cm deep all over. Rub the namak (salt) very generously over every surface and into every cut. Slide into your oven at 80°C (175°F).
After 3 hours, remove the meat from the oven.
Put the dried meat pieces in a large bowl and cover completely with cold pani (water). Cover the bowl and Put in the refrigerator overnight (at least 8 hours, ideally 10-12 hours).
Remove the meat from the soaking water and rinse each piece under cold running water. If it tastes extremely salty, soak for another 2 hours in fresh water and drain again.

Stir in 6 cups of fresh pani (water). Stir in all the whole spices: badi elaichi (black cardamom), laung (cloves), kali mirch (black peppercorns), darchini (cinnamon), tez patta (bay leaves), and zeera (cumin seeds). Do NOT Stir in salt yet — the meat still has salt inside it.
Put the pot over high heat and bring to a rolling boil. As the water heats up, a grey-brown foam will form on the surface — this is protein and impurities coming out of the meat.

Once the foam has been skimmed, reduce the heat to low. The liquid should be at a gentle simmer — small lazy bubbles rising, not a vigorous boil. Cover the pot partially (leave a small gap for steam to escape) and cook for 2 to 2.5 hours.
After 2 hours, test the meat by pressing a thick piece with a spoon. If the meat is still tough, continue cooking for another 30 minutes and test again.
